speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Subsequently, we will still move and take the second and third Motions separately in compliance with Parliamentary procedural requirements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As part of its mandate to ensure the stability of the international monetary system, the IMF provides financial assistance to countries experiencing balance of payments difficulties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To carry out its functions, the IMF relies on resources provided by member countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Arising from the COVID-19 pandemic, the IMF has seen a surge in requests for financial assistance, especially from low-income countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: IMF has, therefore, called on its members to help bolster its financial resources to assist the most vulnerable members in recovering from the severe impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, approved by Parliament on 11 July 2016, enables MAS to make grants to the IMF as part of international efforts to assist low-income countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is subject to three conditions, as specified under the Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, such financial assistance is part of a collective action amongst IMF member countries; second, MAS publicly discloses key information about the financial assistance; and third, Parliament fixes, by resolution, the maximum amount of the grants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will now explain the context and considerations for the three grants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, Singapore's grant to the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, or CCRT.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The CCRT was established in 2015 to provide debt relief to the IMF's poorest and most vulnerable members in the event of a natural catastrophe or global health pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The relief on debt service will free up scarce financial resources to continue strengthening the eligible countries' medical care capacities and address the social and economic fallout from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The CCRT is in urgent need of replenishment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since the onset of the pandemic, the IMF has disbursed over US$500 million in debt relief to CCRT-eligible members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the pre-COVID balance has been completely depleted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The disbursements were made possible through the additional contributions by other member countries, which has amounted to US$800 million so far.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This represents about 1.2% of the total amount of US$1.4 billion or SDR 1 billion, needed to replenish the CCRT.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore's contribution is based on our quota share at the IMF and similar to how other countries' contributions are determined.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, the COVID-19 Crisis Capacity Development Initiative, or CCCDI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore's grant to the newly launched CCCDI will help to meet the urgent capacity development needs of countries affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The objective of the CCCDI is to help these countries develop effective policies to mitigate the economic impact of the pandemic and support economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This comes in the form of technical advice, practical tools and policy-oriented training to build skills to manage the crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: IMF has reached out to member countries, including Singapore, to seek funding support for the CCCDI, and suggested that Singapore make a contribution of between US$2 million to US$4 million.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It represents 2% of the total amount of US$100 million needed to support the CCCDI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, contribution to the trust for Special Poverty Reduction and Growth Operations for the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries for Somalia's debt relief, or PRG-HIPC Trust.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Trust will provide support for the debt relief of Somalia, which is in urgent need of assistance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The majority of IMF member countries, including the ASEAN-4 countries, namely, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines and Thailand, have already committed to contributing to Somalia's debt relief package.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore already holds funds in the other IMF accounts to cover overdue payments incurred by members which are unable to pay and the contribution will be drawn from these accounts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore's contribution would form approximately 0.3% of the IMF's financing package of US$344 million (or SDR 242 million) for Somalia's debt relief.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why are we making these contributions to the causes of the IMF?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In short, we live in an interdependent world and Singapore needs to do its part.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Particularly, the COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the need for decisive and urgent collective actions to manage global crises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As a highly open economy, Singapore has a strong stake in ensuring that the world contain the pandemic, restore people-to-people connections across the world and support global economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By contributing to the three funds I have mentioned above, we can play our part as a stakeholder of the international community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As explained earlier, the grant to the PRG-HIPC Trust will not affect the size of Singapore's Official Foreign Reserves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The proposed grant amounts are also reasonable and commensurate with Singapore's position and role in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Following Parliament's resolution to fix the maximum amount of grants that MAS can allocate to the IMF's CCRT, CCCDI and PRG-HIPC Trust, MAS will publish in the Gazette key information about the grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I will go further: as a country that has historically hung its hat and been a major beneficiary from globalisation, I would argue that doing so goes beyond responsibility, and is instead a duty and an obligation on our part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, we are not doing enough and I wish to explain why we should do more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should, of course, state at the outset that I have previously worked for seven years in the trenches as an economist in a Bretton Woods Institution and I maintain a small balance in my self-funded group retirement account and the staff account at the credit union.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I do not receive nor maintain any direct financial interests in the Bank nor the Fund.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor do we have any concerted strategy for increasing our representation at international organisations, such as the United Nations (UN).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Compare this to the 506 staff sent by Sweden, a country about twice our size, or the 559 sent by Denmark with a population comparable to ours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of our citizens are narrowly affiliated with just two institutions – the IMF and the World Bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Apocryphally, this position was motivated by our founding father, former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew, who was reluctant to risk the brain drain that could result when our talents went abroad to work at these international institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our legacy of ambivalence extends to our pocketbook.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Remarkably, the official reason for our unwillingness to extend official aid is because, and I quote, "Singapore is a developing country and does not provide official development assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We undertake South-South capacity building programmes with other developing countries." The multiple rounds of assistance offered under the aegis of the Singapore Cooperation Programme has, undeniably, been welcomed by other nations in need, but it is befuddling that we would remain unwilling to extend financial resources to other countries, beyond merely technical assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, Singapore has also largely eschewed the receipt of foreign aid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But even so, historical development assistance inflows have come to a non-trivial amount.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This amount, while uncorrected for inflation, nevertheless represents a net receipt of funds from the international community over the course of our modern history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This amount actually far exceeds the comparatively small amounts that we are formally extending to the Fund today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, foreign aid has a mixed record and there is no clear evidence that foreign aid can reliably raise economic growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Often, the reason is because of politics: donor countries tie aid to specific requirements, which may not be the most beneficial use for the recipient country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or the governments which receive such foreign aid become more responsive to their foreign benefactors, as opposed to their own people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But by the same token, aid can be effective when it is conditional, albeit not by making it contingent on certain uses specified by the donor, but by extending support to countries that we observe exercise good policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Aid can also be channelled to responsible multilateral organisations with a good track record of ensuring that the funds they receive are properly utilised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if we are still reticent to provide aid because it would be managed by external parties, we can always direct the funds towards the formation of an international volunteer corps tasked to provide social and economic development assistance to other countries, especially those in ASEAN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the key, as in all good investments, is to carefully direct our foreign aid dollars towards initiatives that take into account returns but adjusted for risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, countries, such as Luxembourg and the United Kingdom, demonstrate that it is possible to be simultaneously generous, as well as principled, in one's foreign aid practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must take care of our own needs first and we should prioritise these needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In crisis times, this is even more pertinent, as many Singaporeans are facing hard times and it is difficult to convince them that we should be looking out for the well-being of those in other nations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When citizens from countries around the world are asked how much they think their country contributes, they systematically over-estimate this amount, compared to actual disbursements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, we are certainly not unique in wanting to look out for ourselves first, and all the more during crisis times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But generosity has its own reward and I believe that we are more than capable of doing both.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not think that just because we are in crisis mode, we neglect planning for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And that future must, surely, entail thinking about the performance of economies besides our own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because even from a purely self-interested perspective, uplifting our neighbouring economies can pay dividends in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, what we export shows up as another country's imports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when their incomes are elevated, their consumers are better able to afford our goods and services, which skew towards those of higher value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Netherlands, Switzerland, Qatar and the UAE know that they are able to punch above their weight because they have invested in multilateral organisations and in the international system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if we establish a formal international volunteer corps, the experience gained by our returning volunteers will also contribute toward our goal of promoting greater sensitivity toward regional integration efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given how citizens' perceptions are that donor governments give more than they actually do, it seems like a short logical step to infer that what they generally want is less, not more foreign aid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reason, I think, is because we are fundamentally social creatures, and some degree of reciprocity and altruism is baked into our moral fibre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are often willing to help those less well-off than we are, so long as we can afford it and so long as we are assured that the money is well-spent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if we accept this premise, then I would submit that a more concerted effort to increase our official development assistance is essentially a problem to be resolved, rather than an insurmountable obstacle.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: COVID-19 respect no borders or jurisdictions and all countries, big or small, strong or vulnerable, do get impacted in one way or another and we are in this together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In particular, countries in a better position should do our part to help those that face difficulties during the crisis, including the economic fall-out from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the thick of the pandemic last year, Singapore stepped up to contribute diagnostic test kits, PCR machines, protective gears, thermal scanners to neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is all part of the collective global action to help the most vulnerable countries during this major humanitarian crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The IMF is the most suitable international agency to carry out these efforts given its multilateral platforms as well as expertise, organisation and their suite of programmes available.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The IMF has always been among the key financing agencies to ensure stability of the international monetary system such as assisting countries with the balance of payments difficulty.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As an international financial centre and a global trade node, Singapore's interest is best served when there are financial stabilities, stronger monetary cooperation amongst countries and sustainable economic growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I can imagine that as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: IMF would have been inundated with more requests for assistance, especially from the low-income countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Not withstanding my support, can I ask the Minister a couple of questions?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: By contributing to these three funds, we will play our part as responsible stakeholders of these international communities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So with that, I support the three Motions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Just has been the case domestically, COVID-19 is disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable countries internationally.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The impact on health, education, food security, and livelihoods is staggering.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Millions of children are at risk as routine vaccination programmes have had to be deprioritized and more children are also dropping out of school, especially girls.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, protecting the vulnerable is needed to fight this global pandemic, fuel global economic recovery and growth, and to maintain social stability and peace.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The successful and inclusive response now can set us all up for a better future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, there is, as my colleagues have said, a clear, moral and economic imperative for private, public and social sectors to work together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, we have seen the continued rise of nationalism and protectionism, and multilateralism continues to weaken.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Declining levels of official development assistance and rising levels of debt are also impeding the world's ability to pay for efforts to realise global sustainable development goals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is acutely aware of the connectedness and the importance of multilateral efforts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Multilateral cooperation and multilateral institutions like the IMF remain the best way to tackle global challenges, whether it is COVID-19, future pandemics, economic slowdown or climate change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have also seen what remarkable things can be achieved when the world does come together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So it is important to rebuild and recommit to multilateralism.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am also heartened by two aspects of the proposed support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope that the IMF will also be flexible and responsive in the detailed design and implementation to address any potential stakeholder concerns and maintain support for the grants from member countries and recipients.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And just as Prime Minister Lee's call helped to shape the global conversation around equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines, that the voices of our leaders such as Senior Minister Tharman, will help shape how the world helps low-income countries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond increasing our development assistance though, I would like to propose two strategies to go in parallel.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The first is to increase awareness and appreciation of our international assistance efforts among our people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our youths have grown up in a connected world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They understand intuitively the imperative for us to do more to assist the most vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, we must show the next generation that we are listening and that we have heard them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And for the skeptics, we must continue to demonstrate to our people that our international assistance efforts can make us all better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This will help our people understand the region better and support our regionalisation and internationalisation efforts, bring us back to where I started, that the world is interconnected.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we take a step back, the reason is really that we live in an interconnected world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And so, it is in Singapore's interest to be part of this international community where we work together, where we cooperate, where there are rules, there are norms, there are best practices that hold every country into account to ensure that we live peacefully together in a global village.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in such a system there will be benefits, there will be obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And on balance for a small city-state like us, the benefits far outweigh the obligations and the costs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, it is existential for us to live in such a global international cooperation system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we want to do this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore is represented in the Board through the voting group of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And so, we get an update and from time to time the IMF would publish reports, to update on the progress of all these funds.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And in fact, I think what he has just described, is 50 over years of foreign policy and one of our key tenets – which is we want our neighbours to all do well, we want our region to do well.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That way, there is global cooperation that a small country like us, can also do well.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Which is why for so many years, we contribute on various international fora, whatever we can do within our means as a small country.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we talked about IMF, but for many years, MFA had the Singapore Cooperation Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We do not contribute money per se, but we run so many training programmes and invite government officials, representatives of NGOs and other organisations to come to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We provide necessary training, they take reference on what we do, we learn from each other.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I can see that whether it is ICAO or IMO, we have participated in all kinds of capacity building programmes, contributing to the greater common good.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We talked about the Paris Agreement, we had launched the Green Plan and had a long debate on the Motion on climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we too, contribute to the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our contribution is always commensurate with our size.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think it is important for us to contribute and it is beyond money.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We learn by doing, and whatever we have learned, we share with the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And sometimes, those are the lessons that are priceless.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Likewise, we learn those lessons from others and those are priceless.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim did say we should increase our monetary contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the IMF, it goes by your voting rights and your quota.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, of course, if you contribute more, the fiscal burden is higher and it has to be funded by tax collections as well.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For us, as a small country, our stance is better not to go around to say that we have all these resources, we can give out more money.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But instead, we are always struggling for relevance, always fighting to earn a living.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And along the way, we learn many lessons and we can share those lessons with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think this is a better way for Singapore to contribute to the common good and the larger global society.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Mariam Jafaar gave a couple of good suggestions on raising awareness and educating the broader public including businesses on the work that we do internationally and how much Singapore can help.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When MAS put out our press release on these IMF contributions, it was a little bit disappointing because if you look through the threads, there were quite a few criticisms saying, "Why is Singapore giving out money to other countries?" Frankly, within MAS, when we reviewed that, we were a little bit disappointed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I am quite glad that today, all the Members that stood up and spoke about this, supported this contribution to the IMF grants.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It shows that as a small country, we can also be big-hearted, that we can also play our role.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think we also share our concern for the future of humanity and we will do our part.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What Ms Mariam Jafaar suggested is a good idea and we will see what we can do to raise awareness of what we can do internationally.
